_README: Commonly studied dose ranges used by Dose Lab, from human trials in healthy adults, summarised for teaching. These are NOT universally correct doses and NOT personalised: the right amount depends on the ingredient, formulation, population, goal and the state of the evidence, and reputable sources disagree at the margins. Corrections are welcome by pull request - please cite a source.

_fields.unit: Unit the effectiveDose figures are expressed in.
_fields.mgPerUnit: Multiplier converting one unit to milligrams. Drives the blend arithmetic.
_fields.evidence: strong | moderate | weak | none | caution. 'none' means no dose has been shown to produce the marketed effect. 'caution' means the concern is excess rather than shortfall.
_fields.colour: Powder colour in the 3D view. Cosmetic only.
_fields.review: status: unverified | verified | corrected. source: a citation for referenceRange - a DOI, PubMed ID, an ISSN position stand, or an Examine.com page. Nothing here has been checked by a qualified person yet; see REVIEW.md.
_fields.referenceRange: The commonly studied dose range from human trials in healthy adults. `low` is the threshold the tool compares a label against; `high` is shown alongside it so the reader sees a range rather than a single number. There is no universally correct dose for a supplement - it depends on the ingredient, formulation, population and goal - so the tool reports this range and never asserts that a given amount 'is effective'.

caffeine.name: Caffeine anhydrous
caffeine.mechanism: Blocks adenosine, so fatigue signalling is muted. The most reliably effective ergogenic aid there is.
caffeine.note: Roughly 3-6 mg per kg of bodyweight. Above about 400 mg in one sitting the returns stop and the side effects don't.

betaAlanine.name: Beta-alanine
betaAlanine.mechanism: Raises muscle carnosine, which buffers the acidity that ends a hard set. Helps most in the 60-240 second effort range.
betaAlanine.note: Works by saturating muscle carnosine over weeks, so a single dose does nothing acutely. The tingle is not the effect.

citrulline.name: L-Citrulline
citrulline.mechanism: Converts to arginine in the kidneys and raises nitric oxide, improving blood flow and reducing perceived effort.
citrulline.note: One of the most reliably underdosed ingredients in the category, because it is expensive and bulky.

citMalate.name: Citrulline malate (2:1)
citMalate.mechanism: Citrulline plus malate, an intermediate in aerobic energy production. Dosed higher because only part of the weight is citrulline.
citMalate.note: A 2:1 blend is only two-thirds citrulline, so 8 g of citrulline malate delivers about 5.3 g of citrulline.

creatine.name: Creatine monohydrate
creatine.mechanism: Regenerates ATP during short maximal efforts. Adds reps at the top end and increases total training volume over time.
creatine.note: The most studied sports supplement there is. Monohydrate is the researched form; the exotic ones cost more and do not outperform it.

betaine.name: Betaine anhydrous
betaine.mechanism: An osmolyte that helps cells hold water under load, with modest evidence for power output.
betaine.note: Effective doses in trials sit between 2,400 and 4,000 mg taken before training.

taurine.name: Taurine
taurine.mechanism: Regulates calcium handling and cell volume in working muscle. Mild but consistently measurable.
taurine.note: Cheap, well tolerated, and frequently included at a fraction of the trial dose.

tyrosine.name: L-Tyrosine
tyrosine.mechanism: A precursor to dopamine and noradrenaline, which get depleted under acute stress.
tyrosine.note: Evidence is for acute stress and sleep deprivation rather than for training performance.

theanine.name: L-Theanine
theanine.mechanism: Raises alpha wave activity. Paired with caffeine it keeps the alertness and removes the edge.
theanine.note: Usually paired with caffeine at roughly 1:1 to 2:1 to blunt the jitter.

alphaGPC.name: Alpha-GPC
alphaGPC.mechanism: A choline source that crosses into the brain, used for acetylcholine synthesis and power output.
alphaGPC.note: One of the few nootropic additions with a defensible dose range.

ashwagandha.name: Ashwagandha extract
ashwagandha.mechanism: An adaptogen with reasonable evidence for lowering cortisol and perceived stress.
ashwagandha.note: Trials use standardised root extracts. An unstandardised powder at 50 mg is not the same product.

rhodiola.name: Rhodiola rosea
rhodiola.mechanism: Studied for fatigue resistance and perceived exertion rather than raw strength.
rhodiola.note: Standardised to rosavins and salidroside; unstandardised material tells you nothing.

beetroot.name: Beetroot extract
beetroot.mechanism: A nitrate source. Nitrate converts to nitric oxide and lowers the oxygen cost of submaximal work.
beetroot.note: What matters is the nitrate content, which most labels do not declare at all.

hmb.name: HMB
hmb.mechanism: A leucine metabolite studied for limiting muscle breakdown during hard training or a deficit.
hmb.note: Trial dose is 3 g. Benefits look real in untrained people and largely vanish in trained ones.

arginine.name: L-Arginine
arginine.mechanism: Intended as a nitric oxide precursor, but most of an oral dose is destroyed before it reaches circulation.
arginine.note: Poor oral bioavailability - it is broken down before it does much. Citrulline raises arginine levels more effectively than arginine does.

bcaa.name: BCAAs
bcaa.mechanism: Three amino acids your body cannot make. Already present in every complete protein you eat.
bcaa.note: Largely redundant if daily protein is adequate, because whole protein already contains them.

glutamine.name: L-Glutamine
glutamine.mechanism: The most abundant amino acid in the body. Genuinely useful clinically; hard to show a benefit in healthy trained adults.
glutamine.note: Well evidenced in clinical settings, thin evidence for healthy trained adults.

tribulus.name: Tribulus terrestris
tribulus.mechanism: Marketed as a testosterone booster. Controlled trials do not find that effect.
tribulus.note: Repeatedly tested for raising testosterone and repeatedly found not to. There is no dose that fixes this.

huperzine.name: Huperzine A
huperzine.mechanism: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, so acetylcholine lingers. Active in microgrammes.
huperzine.note: Active in microgrammes, which makes it a cheap way to lengthen an ingredient list.

niacin.name: Niacin (vitamin B3)
niacin.mechanism: An essential B vitamin. In excess it dilates skin capillaries, which is the flush.
niacin.note: The adult RDA is about 16 mg. Doses above that do nothing extra nutritionally, but from roughly 30 mg upward nicotinic acid causes flushing - a warm prickling across the skin that is very often mistaken for the product kicking in.

vitD.name: Vitamin D3
vitD.mechanism: A prohormone made in skin from sunlight. Deficiency is common indoors and at high latitudes.
vitD.note: Meaningful supplementation starts around 1,000 IU for most adults.

magnesium.name: Magnesium
magnesium.mechanism: A cofactor in hundreds of enzyme reactions including muscle contraction and sleep regulation.
magnesium.note: Elemental magnesium, not the weight of the salt. Magnesium oxide is roughly 4% absorbed - the cheapest form on the shelf.

zinc.name: Zinc
zinc.mechanism: Essential for immune function and hormone production. Lost in sweat, so athletes run low more often.
zinc.note: Upper limit is about 40 mg a day; chronic excess interferes with copper.

omega3.name: EPA + DHA
omega3.mechanism: Long-chain fats that regulate the inflammatory response and are structural in cell membranes.
omega3.note: Read the EPA and DHA figures, not the total fish oil weight. A 1,000 mg capsule often carries 300 mg of actual omega-3.

collagen.name: Collagen peptides
collagen.mechanism: Supplies glycine and proline for connective tissue. Taken with vitamin C before loading the tendon.
collagen.note: Trials use 10-15 g. Anything under a gram is there for the ingredient list.

sodium.name: Sodium
sodium.mechanism: The electrolyte you lose most of in sweat. Drives fluid retention and nerve conduction.
sodium.note: For sweat replacement during long or hot sessions. Context dependent rather than universally needed.
